title: Boss: the clip upload review
summary: A load-test report for a video clip feature: read the consumer lag, size the API for streaming versus direct uploads, make the thumbnail worker idempotent and loop-proof, and price the bucket with lifecycle tiers.

steps.title: The ticket: CLIPS-214, load-test review
body: Short video clips launch next month. The load test from staging came back, and your lead wants a review
before the design is signed off:
LOAD TEST: clips-upload   target: 2,200 uploads/s at peak, average clip 5 MB
api pods (8 vCPU, 10 Gbps)   cpu 22%   net rx saturated at 6 pods   p99 4.1 s   errors 3.2%
thumbnail worker group       lag growing on one partition, the others near 0
thumbnail worker             processed 1.9x more events than uploads
bucket (projected)           100 GB/day of new clips, nothing ever deleted or moved
Four findings to turn into code: where the lag is, how many pods the two upload designs need, why the
worker does almost twice the work, and what the bucket will cost with lifecycle tiers.

steps.title: Where is the lag?
prompt: Write `(long Total, int WorstPartition) Lag(string[] lines)` for `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe` output.
Columns are separated by spaces: `GROUP TOPIC PARTITION CURRENT-OFFSET LOG-END-OFFSET LAG CONSUMER-ID`.
- skip the header (first column `GROUP`), blank lines and notes that start with `(`;
- a partition's lag is the `LAG` column; when it is `-`, use `LOG-END - CURRENT`, or the whole `LOG-END` when
`CURRENT` is also `-` (the group never committed);
- return the total lag and the partition with the largest lag (the lowest partition number on a tie);
with no partitions, `(0, -1)`.
One partition holding most of the lag means a hot key or a stuck consumer, not too few consumers.
solution: if (lag > worstLag || (lag == worstLag && partition < worst)) { worstLag = lag; worst = partition; }
hints: `line.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries)` gives the columns; skip rows whose first column is `GROUP` or starts with `(`.
Keep the worst lag seen so far and its partition; replace it on a larger lag, or an equal lag with a smaller partition number.
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoOut = new[] {
"GROUP       TOPIC    PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG     CONSUMER-ID",
"thumbnails  uploads  0          1000            1200            200     thumbnails-1",
"thumbnails  uploads  1          900             4900            4000    thumbnails-2",
"thumbnails  uploads  2          -               800             -       -",
"thumbnails  uploads  3          500             1300            800     thumbnails-3",
"(2 more members have no partitions assigned)" };
Dojo.Eq("total lag, with the never-committed partition counted in full", (5800L, 1), Lag(dojoOut));
Dojo.Eq("'-' lag with a committed offset is LOG-END minus CURRENT", (300L, 0), Lag(new[] { "g t 0 700 1000 - c-1" }));
Dojo.Eq("a tie goes to the lower partition", (100L, 2), Lag(new[] { "g t 5 0 50 50 c", "g t 2 0 50 50 c" }));
Dojo.Eq("no partitions", (0L, -1), Lag(new[] { "GROUP TOPIC PARTITION CURRENT-OFFSET LOG-END-OFFSET LAG CONSUMER-ID" }));

steps.title: Bandwidth or CPU?
prompt: Write `int PodsNeeded(double rps, double cpuMsPerRequest, int coresPerPod, double maxCpu, double mbPerRequest, double nicGbps, double maxNic)`:
- by CPU: `rps × cpuMsPerRequest / 1000` cores busy, divided by `coresPerPod × maxCpu`, rounded up;
- by network: `rps × mbPerRequest × 8 / 1000` Gbps, divided by `nicGbps × maxNic`, rounded up;
- return the larger, at least 1.
Streaming the clips through the API: 2,200 uploads/s, 4 ms CPU, 8 cores, 60% CPU target, 5 MB each, 10 Gbps
cards at 60%: **15 pods**, all for bandwidth. With presigned direct uploads the API only handles about 2 KB
of JSON per upload: **2 pods**.
starter: int PodsNeeded(double rps, double cpuMsPerRequest, int coresPerPod, double maxCpu, double mbPerRequest, double nicGbps, double maxNic)
solution: int PodsNeeded(double rps, double cpuMsPerRequest, int coresPerPod, double maxCpu, double mbPerRequest, double nicGbps, double maxNic)
hints: MB/s to Gbps: multiply by 8 (bits) and divide by 1,000 (mega to giga).
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("streaming clips through the API: 15 pods for bandwidth", 15, PodsNeeded(2200, 4, 8, 0.6, 5, 10, 0.6));
Dojo.Eq("direct uploads: 2 pods for CPU", 2, PodsNeeded(2200, 4, 8, 0.6, 0.002, 10, 0.6));
Dojo.Eq("a CPU-heavy API is sized by CPU", 23, PodsNeeded(1000, 100, 8, 0.55, 0.01, 10, 0.6));
Dojo.Eq("no traffic still runs one pod", 1, PodsNeeded(0, 4, 8, 0.6, 5, 10, 0.6));

steps.title: An idempotent, loop-proof worker
prompt: The worker did 1.9x more work than there were uploads, for two reasons: events are delivered **at least
once**, and the worker writes its thumbnails into the **same bucket**, under `thumbs/`, which fires another
object-created event for every thumbnail.
Write a class `ThumbnailWorker`:
- `bool Handle(string key, string etag)` returns true when it makes a thumbnail, false when it skips;
- skip keys under `thumbs/` (its own output);
- skip a `(key, etag)` pair it has already handled (a redelivery); a **new etag** for the same key is a
new upload (the object was overwritten) and is handled;
- `List<string> Made` lists each thumbnail made, as `thumbs/{key}` (for example `thumbs/u42/a.mp4`), in order.
starter: public bool Handle(string key, string etag) => false;
solution: readonly HashSet<(string Key, string Etag)> seen = new();
public bool Handle(string key, string etag)
hints: A `HashSet<(string, string)>` remembers handled pairs; `Add` returns false when the pair is already there.
template: var dojoW = new ThumbnailWorker();
Dojo.Check("a new upload is handled", dojoW.Handle("u42/a.mp4", "e1"));
Dojo.Check("a redelivery is skipped", !dojoW.Handle("u42/a.mp4", "e1"));
Dojo.Check("its own thumbnail event is skipped", !dojoW.Handle("thumbs/u42/a.mp4", "t1"));
Dojo.Check("an overwrite (new etag) is handled again", dojoW.Handle("u42/a.mp4", "e2"));
Dojo.Check("another key is independent", dojoW.Handle("u7/b.mp4", "e1"));
Dojo.Eq("three thumbnails made, in order", new List<string> { "thumbs/u42/a.mp4", "thumbs/u42/a.mp4", "thumbs/u7/b.mp4" }, dojoW.Made);
Dojo.Check("a key that only contains thumbs/ later is still handled", dojoW.Handle("u9/thumbs/c.mp4", "e1"));
{{CODE}}

steps.title: Price the bucket with lifecycle tiers
prompt: New clips arrive at a steady `gbPerDay`. Write `double StorageCostPerMonth(double gbPerDay, int daysRunning)`:
the monthly bill after `daysRunning` days, with a lifecycle rule that moves data by age. Each day's batch has
an age from `0` (today) to `daysRunning - 1` and is billed per GB-month at:
| Age in days | Tier | $ per GB-month (illustrative) |
| 0 to 29 | standard | 0.023 |
| 30 to 179 | infrequent access | 0.0125 |
| 180 and over | archive | 0.004 |
Return it rounded to cents (`Math.Round(x, 2)`). After 200 days at 100 GB/day the bill is `264.5`; without
the rule (everything standard) it would be `460`.
hints: Loop over the ages `0 .. daysRunning - 1` and pick the price for each.
Add `gbPerDay × price` for each day's batch, then round once at the end.
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("the first month is all standard", 69.0, StorageCostPerMonth(100, 30));
Dojo.Eq("after 200 days, three tiers", 264.5, StorageCostPerMonth(100, 200));
Dojo.Eq("after a year", 330.5, StorageCostPerMonth(100, 365));
Dojo.Eq("nothing stored yet", 0.0, StorageCostPerMonth(100, 0));
Dojo.Eq("one day of data", 2.3, StorageCostPerMonth(100, 1));

steps.title: Build it: photo sharing
prompt: In the **System design board**, open the capstone *Photo sharing*. You start from the users alone. Put the
uploads into **object storage** with presigned URLs, serve photos through a **CDN**, cache the feed reads,
spread the servers over availability zones, and meet the latency, availability and budget goals.
steps.explain: The bytes never touch your app servers or your database: the bucket takes the uploads, the CDN serves the views, and your own servers only handle small JSON. That is what keeps the bill and the p99 down.
